The Later 1960s

The Republic at Full Volume

Assassinations and moon landings. Protest chants and children's songs. The decade did not end by solving America. It ended by revealing it.

scroll on, friend ✿ ↓

CH. 1

Johnson and the Great Society

a wounded country and a stack of unfinished business

President Lyndon B. Johnson, who knew Congress the way a river knows its own bends

After John F. Kennedy was killed in 1963, Lyndon B. Johnson inherited a wounded country and a stack of unfinished business. Johnson was not polished like Kennedy. He was large, forceful, persuasive, and sometimes frighteningly intense. He knew Congress the way a river knows its own bends. Where Kennedy had often sounded like a bright trumpet, Johnson sounded like a hammer hitting law into shape.

Johnson wanted to build what he called the . This meant using the federal government to fight poverty, expand education, improve health care, protect civil rights, and make American life less cruel for people left out of prosperity. In 1964, he declared a , meaning not a literal war with soldiers, but a major government campaign against hunger, poor schools, lack of medical care, and limited opportunity. Programs connected to this era included , , , food assistance expansion, education funding, and community action programs. Johnson's goal was not only to reduce poverty but to change the conditions that helped keep people poor.

But the Great Society had two shadows. One shadow was political: not everyone agreed that the federal government should have such a large role in social life. The other shadow was Vietnam. Johnson tried to build schools and hospitals at home while sending more troops into war overseas. It was like trying to raise a cathedral while the ground beneath it cracked.

"The later 1960s became a story of two Americas moving at once: one trying to widen democracy, the other falling deeper into violence and distrust."
✿ ☮ ✿ ☮ ✿

Pause & Reflect

Before reading on, sit with what you just read. Active recall and short reflection breaks help your brain move new ideas from short-term to long-term memory.

  • What was Johnson trying to build with the Great Society? Try to explain it without looking back at the passage.
  • The text describes the Great Society as having "two shadows." What were they, and which shadow do you think was bigger?
CH. 2

The Vote, Malcolm X, and Thurgood Marshall

civil rights moves from protest signs into law itself

Demonstrators at the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom

The civil rights movement did not stop with the Civil Rights Act of 1964. In many Southern states, Black citizens were still blocked from voting through , , intimidation, violence, and unfair local rules. The of 1965 was designed to enforce the , which had promised that citizens could not be denied the vote because of race. The law gave the federal government stronger power to stop discriminatory voting practices, especially in places with long records of suppression.

This was not simply paperwork. Voting meant power: sheriffs, judges, school boards, mayors, governors, and presidents. A person who could not vote could be ruled but not truly represented.

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. casts a ballot, Coretta Scott King at his side

At the same time, the civil rights movement was not one single voice. Martin Luther King Jr. preached nonviolent protest and integration. , especially before his break with the Nation of Islam, spoke in sharper tones about Black self-defense, racial pride, and the failures of white America. He criticized the idea that Black people should patiently wait for justice from institutions that had abused them for centuries. After his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1964, Malcolm X's views became more international and, in some ways, more open to cooperation across racial lines, though he remained fiercely critical of racism. He was assassinated on February 21, 1965, in New York City. His death removed one of the decade's most forceful and unsettling voices.

Malcolm X

Justice Thurgood Marshall

Then came , a lawyer who had already helped change American history before he ever joined the Supreme Court. Marshall had argued civil rights cases for the Legal Defense Fund and was central to the legal fight against school segregation, including . In 1967, Johnson nominated him to the U.S. Supreme Court. Marshall became the first Black Supreme Court justice, a major milestone in the long struggle to move civil rights from protest signs into law itself.

✿ ☮ ✿ ☮ ✿

Quick Recall ✷

Tap your answer. Instant feedback helps lock the idea in.

1. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 was designed to enforce which amendment?
Right on. The Fifteenth Amendment had promised the vote could not be denied because of race, but states had been ignoring it for nearly a century.
2. Who became the first Black Supreme Court justice?
Far out. Marshall had already won Brown v. Board of Education before he ever wore the robe.
3. Which method was used in Southern states to block Black citizens from voting?
Yes. These tools, plus intimidation, kept Black voters off the rolls until 1965 finally put real federal teeth into the law.
CH. 3

Vietnam: The War That Ate the Decade

jungle, money, soldiers, television, doubt

Vietnam, divided at the 17th parallel since 1954

The Vietnam War began before Johnson, but under Johnson it grew into a massive American war. Vietnam had been divided into communist North Vietnam and anti-communist South Vietnam. The United States supported South Vietnam because American leaders believed that if one country fell to communism, others might follow. This idea was called the .

U.S. destroyer at sea, the kind of ship reportedly attacked in the Gulf of Tonkin

In 1964, after reported attacks on U.S. ships in the Gulf of Tonkin, Congress passed the , giving Johnson broad authority to increase U.S. involvement in Vietnam. The resolution became a major legal foundation for escalation. In 1965, U.S. troop levels rose sharply, and the war became more visible in American homes through television news.

American soldiers and Huey helicopters in Vietnam

For a sixth grader, the key point is this: Vietnam was not just "America versus communism." It was also a civil war inside Vietnam, a Cold War conflict between global powers, a struggle over independence after colonial rule, and a test of American military power. That is why it became so difficult. The U.S. had planes, helicopters, money, and soldiers, but it could not easily defeat an enemy fighting on familiar ground with political support in parts of the population.

As the war dragged on, more Americans protested. Some believed the war was necessary to stop communism. Others believed it was immoral, unwinnable, or based on false assumptions. Young men faced the , meaning they could be required to serve in the military. College campuses became centers of protest. Families split at dinner tables. The nightly news carried images of fire, jungle, body bags, and villages.

"The Great Society promised repair. Vietnam delivered rupture."
✿ ☮ ✿ ☮ ✿

Pause & Reflect

The text says Vietnam was at least four wars at once. Stop here and try to name them in your own words. Studies on learning show that retrieving information (pulling it out of your head) makes it stick far better than just rereading.

  • Why did the U.S. believe it had to support South Vietnam? Use the term "domino theory" in your answer.
  • Imagine you are a college student in 1968 watching the news. What would make you decide to support the war, or to protest it?
CH. 4

1968: The Year the Country Shattered

if the 1960s were a storm, 1968 was the year the roof came loose

The balcony at the Lorraine Motel, Memphis, April 4, 1968

If the 1960s were a storm, 1968 was the year the roof came loose.

On April 4, 1968, Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee, where he had gone to support striking sanitation workers. King was 39 years old. His death sparked grief, anger, and uprisings in cities across the United States. For many Americans, it felt as if the country had murdered one of its own prophets. The National Archives continues to maintain and release records related to King's assassination, reflecting the lasting public importance and controversy surrounding the event.

The morning after Robert F. Kennedy was shot in Los Angeles

Just two months later, on June 5, 1968, Robert F. Kennedy was shot in Los Angeles after winning the California Democratic presidential primary. He died the next day. RFK had become a symbol for many people who opposed the Vietnam War and wanted renewed attention to poverty and racial justice. His assassination deepened the feeling that the nation had entered a dark corridor with no clear exit. The National Archives also maintains records related to RFK's assassination.

That same year, American politics turned hard and bitter. Protests erupted outside the Democratic National Convention in Chicago. Police beat demonstrators on television. Many voters wanted order; many others wanted justice. Some wanted both but no longer trusted anyone to deliver either.

Richard Nixon at the 1968 Republican National Convention

In November 1968, Richard Nixon was elected president. Nixon had been vice president under Eisenhower, lost the presidency in 1960, and lost the California governor's race in 1962. His 1968 victory was a political comeback. He appealed to what he called the , Americans who were tired of disorder, protest, and rapid change. The election did not end the turmoil. It marked a turn toward a new political age.

✿ ☮ ✿ ☮ ✿

Quick Recall ✷

One more round before the closing chapter.

1. Where was Martin Luther King Jr. when he was assassinated in 1968?
Yes. He had traveled there to support striking sanitation workers.
2. Robert F. Kennedy was shot the night he won which state's Democratic primary?
Correct. The shooting happened at a hotel in Los Angeles right after his victory speech.
3. Which group did Nixon describe as the "silent majority"?
Right. It was a political appeal to people who wanted order more than they wanted further upheaval.
CH. 5

Moonrise, Music, Machines & Sesame Street

strange new doors keep opening, even in the middle of war

Even in the middle of war and mourning, the late 1960s kept opening strange new doors.

Earthrise, photographed by Apollo 8 in December 1968

In December 1968, became the first crewed mission to orbit the Moon. Astronauts Frank Borman, Jim Lovell, and William Anders traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them. They saw the far side of the Moon and photographed , an image of Earth rising over the lunar surface. That picture made Earth look small, blue, fragile, and alone. It helped shape the environmental imagination of the modern age.

An astronaut salutes the flag on the Moon

Then, on July 20, 1969, landed on the Moon. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the lunar surface while Michael Collins orbited above. This was a Cold War achievement, a scientific achievement, and a human myth made real: people had left Earth and stood on another world. NASA describes Apollo as a program whose goals went beyond landing astronauts; it tested technology, human endurance, and national capability.

The Woodstock crowd, August 1969, on a dairy farm in Bethel, New York

Back on Earth, another gathering took place: , held August 15 to 18, 1969, on a farm in Bethel, New York. It became the most famous rock festival of the 1960s, with performers including Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, the Who, Sly and the Family Stone, the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane, and others. Woodstock symbolized youth culture, antiwar feeling, experimentation, music, and the hope, not always realistic, that a different kind of society might be possible.

Festival-goers at Woodstock

Jimi Hendrix on stage

An early ARPANET diagram

In October 1969, another quieter revolution began when the first message was sent over , an experimental computer network funded by the U.S. Defense Department. The intended message was "login," but the system crashed after "lo." That small broken syllable became part of the origin story of the internet.

Mainframe computing in the late 1960s

Then, on November 10, 1969, premiered. It used television, music, humor, animation, puppets, and research-based teaching to help young children learn letters, numbers, social skills, and cultural understanding. The Smithsonian describes it as innovative and radical for its time.

The original Sesame Street cast with Big Bird

"The 1960s did not end by solving America. They ended by revealing it: brilliant, wounded, inventive, divided, and still unfinished."

Final Reflection

Take five minutes here. The decade closed with contradictions stacked on top of contradictions. Try to hold them all in your head at the same time.

  • The text calls Earthrise an image that "helped shape the environmental imagination of the modern age." What do you think it means by that?
  • If you could rewind to one moment from 1968 or 1969 and witness it in person, which would you pick, and why?
  • Pick one word that captures the late 1960s for you. Defend it.
